subject: zeppelin
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: passenger zeppelin with gondola.
Style: art deco.
reasoning:
I'm thinking this should be a static prop model—a passenger zeppelin with an art deco gondola—built as plain geometry under the root group without any joints, since it doesn't need articulation.

I'm weighing how it should rest: real zeppelins on the ground touch down via a bumper wheel under the gondola, so I'll align that contact point to y=0 to satisfy the "stands on ground" requirement. Scale-wise, something like the full Hindenburg at 245 m is accurate but may be excessive for texture density purposes, so I'm leaning toward a smaller real reference like the Graf Zeppelin LZ127 to keep texel density reasonable while still being true-to-life.

I'll settle on a hull around 160 m long and 34 m in diameter, with a gondola somewhat oversized relative to real proportions (about 30 m long, 8 m tall) to push the stylization a bit while keeping it grounded in realistic scale, and I'll make sure lift/tolerance values for decals and surface details are set explicitly rather than left as defaults given the larger size.

Now I'm working out the orientation and construction approach: the zeppelin faces +Z with the nose forward, and the hull is built as a lathe revolved around the Z axis using a defined radius/height profile, with the gondola positioned below the hull near ground level.

I'll use a faceted ngon cross-section, like 16-18 sides, to mimic the authentic polygonal girder structure of real zeppelins, then paint girder lines at the vertex angles (every 22.5°) to highlight the panels. Now I'm shaping the hull profile itself, aiming for a blunt ellipsoidal nose that tapers toward the max diameter.

Writing hull radius function...

For the paint scheme, I'm leaning toward a classic art deco palette—silver or aluminum dope with cream accents.

I'm working out decal orientation on both hull flanks so the "AURORA" lettering reads correctly without mirroring, checking which direction each side's viewer faces relative to the nose.

Now I'm planning the art deco sunburst roundel emblem near the nose and the four cruciform tail fins with striping and hinge lines, making sure the bottom fin's lowest extent clears the gondola's wheel bumper.

Checking the tail fin position — hull radius there is roughly 7.9, and with fin span reaching about 14 from the axis, the bottom edge lands near y=11.5, comfortably clear of the ground. Now I'm setting up the fin geometry itself, defining orientation vectors for the top and bottom fins relative to the hull axis.

Computing the fin outline...

Checking that the fin tip sits well clear of the hull radius at that cross-section, and that the bottom fin stays above the ground line. For paint, I'm planning a navy base with gold pinstripes on the fins to keep the art deco theme, with the rudder/elevator in a separate contrasting color on the trailing edge.

Now I'm turning to the engine nacelles — four teardrop-shaped pusher-propeller gondolas mounted on struts along the lower rear hull, with chrome cowl rings and four-blade propellers with spinners, positioned in pairs at two points along the hull's length.

For the main control car, I'm designing an art-deco streamlined gondola with a stepped bridge, wraparound front windows, and a passenger deck, built as a lofted body tapering from rounded nose to tapered rear. I'm painting it cream with navy lower trim and thin gold speed lines wrapping the nose, plus a decal row of rounded art-deco windows with gold frames along the sides.

I'm working out the vertical positioning so the gondola's top edge sinks slightly into the hull's underside, solving for the center height that puts the bottom near the wheels while overlapping the hull bottom by a small margin for a seated, embedded look.

But since the hull curves, its lower edge rises toward the nose and tail, so I'm checking the gap at the gondola's front end where the hull is narrower — the gap grows to roughly 1.4m there, meaning I'll need a connecting fairing or pylon bridging the gondola to the hull along its length rather than relying on a single fixed overlap.

I'm thinking of lofting a stepped art-deco fairing from the gondola roof up into the hull — sizing it so its top sits around y=11, tall enough to tuck under the hull's bottom curve and read visually as the keel structure. I might also shorten the gondola to around 24m centered near z=18 to simplify the fit, but I'll settle on exact numbers later — possibly favoring a design with window-lined decks built into the hull's lower bottom instead.

For the gondola itself, I'll give it a wraparound bridge window using a nose-mounted glowing decal, plus side window rows per flank, and I'm considering using horizontal surface loops around the gondola to create thin gold speed-stripe rings — maybe three stacked pinstripes for that art-deco triple-banding look.

I'm also planning a small entrance door decal with a fan motif, and a front bumper wheel setup — torus or cylinder touching the ground with fork struts for a pneumatic landing bumper.

I considered adding a rear tail wheel too, like the real Hindenburg had under its bottom fin, but the strut length makes it awkward given the fin's height, so I'll skip it and let the front wheel be the sole resting point since this is meant to look like a hovering airship anyway. I'm now adding a navy keel strip along the gondola's underside.

For the nose, I'm designing an art deco chrome cap with concentric rings, radial ribs, and a mooring point, similar to the battens real zeppelins had along their nose — working out how to use the hull's surface-line paths and slice just the tip section to place these ring details correctly.

I'm adding gold rib battens radiating from the nose cap for that sunburst art deco effect, a chrome nose dome, and navigation lights — red on the port fin tip, green on the starboard, white on the tail — plus painted hull frame lines and a decal strip of passenger windows along the lower hull flank, Hindenburg-style.

Now I'm layering on name banners near the hull's upper front, winged sunburst emblem roundels on the fin side faces, and detailing the engine nacelles with painted metal bodies, chrome cowl rings, mechanic gondola windows, and streamlined struts connecting them to the hull.

I'm also designing the propeller assembly with a conical hub spinner and four rotated blades, considering a rear pusher setup, and planning red control surfaces with gold trim for the elevators and rudders. I'm avoiding the Hindenburg's historical tail markings in favor of a navy fin with a gold sunburst emblem and cream band, and thinking through whether to add joints for propeller rotation and rudder hinges to make the model riggable for animation.

Leaf joints without children risk grabbing nearby geometry unintentionally, which seems fragile. I think static is the safer, simpler choice here since the priority is visual quality, not articulation — glow and decals both work fine on static parts anyway. One thing to watch: with a 128m model, the default decal lift could cause z-fighting at distance, so I should reduce it.

I'm calculating paint texel density: the hull area comes out to roughly 10,000 m² total, and at 2048 resolution that gives about 17 texels/m (6cm detail), which is enough for the pinstripe widths I want. I'll use a 2048 paint atlas, trimmed to the used height, with flat areas compressed in the UV charts.

Now I'm listing out the decal textures needed — names, windows, emblems — aiming for 5-12 total, starting with an art-deco "AURORA" name banner in gold on navy.

I'm sketching the rest of the decal set: a sunburst roundel emblem, glowing window strips for the hull passenger deck, gondola promenade, and bridge wraparound, plus a fan-style door, nacelle grille/chrome details, a registration lettering decal, and maybe a chevron flourish — landing around 8 textures total.

Now I'm estimating part count, targeting somewhere between 180 and 340 pieces, starting with the hull as a single painted sweep.

I'm continuing the parts breakdown: nose battens, cap, mooring ring, tail cone and light, four fins with rudders/elevators, leading-edge trim sweeps, tip lights, emblem decals, plus a few gold art-deco bands looping around the hull near the nose, then hull decals (names, emblems, window strips, registration) and the engine car components.

Now I'm detailing each engine car — lathe body, cowl ring, spinner, four blades, two struts with fairing feet, nacelle window decals, exhaust, and a tail fin — roughly fourteen pieces repeated across all four nacelles, then moving into the gondola: lofted body and fairing, speed-stripe loops, window and bridge decals, door decals, a wheeled bumper assembly, keel, rear observation window, front chevron fender, antennas, and a glowing searchlight tucked under the nose, plus an art-deco roof ornament.

Adding chrome band decals to the gondola nose and a row of small ventilation hoods along the dorsal line of the hull, while skipping mooring ropes, flags, catwalks, and rivet detailing to keep things simple. I'm landing on roughly 150-200 total parts, aiming for the 200 mark, with a 60k triangle budget guiding how I sweep the hull using a 16-sided ngon.

Now I'm setting up the core dimensions and constants for the hull sweep, defining its length, radius, and axis height, then working out the frame orientation so the sweep runs correctly along the Z-axis with the right cap radii at each end.

Writing hull radius function...

At the tip, the radius comes out to about 2.94, so the nose cap extends that far beyond ZN, which seems reasonable. I'm also considering using a faceted 16-sided polygon cross-section instead of a smooth one, which would give the hull a nice art deco look with longitudinal girders visible along the surface.

Writing paint shader code...

Working out the orientation: with the tube running toward +Z, 90 degrees corresponds to -X (right side) and 270 to +X. I'm defining the cheatline symmetrically using distance from the belly (a = |deg-180|), placing the navy band at the side with gold pinstripe edges, and tapering the band's width near the ends so it comes to a sharp art deco point.

Now I'm shifting the band's center upward near the nose so it curves into a chevron feeding into the sunburst, with the tail staying thin like a speed line and the width controlled by smoothstep functions for a clean taper, plus a gold pinstripe just outside the navy edge.

I'm also sketching a thinner red oxblood stripe offset from the main navy band, then working out the nose sunburst as alternating gold rays over navy near the tip, with a cream ring marking the transition and raised gold batten ribs along the surface.

For the tail I'm adding a navy cone with gold rings, and along the top a subtle darker catwalk stripe near the dorsal walkway, while the belly stays a lighter cool tone for countershading based on surface normal. I'm structuring this as a paint function returning color values, mixed with a shading helper, and estimating the texel evaluation cost across the hull area to make sure performance stays reasonable.

Now I'm figuring out how the gold battens trace along the hull's ridge lines at specific clock angles, using arc-length paths sliced near the nose section, confirming the 16-sided polygon vertices align with the batten spacing so they sit cleanly on the ridges. I'm also starting to define the nose cap as a lathed shape along the hull's axis, working out the profile outline that caps the end of the hull.

I'm checking whether the cap's base radius matches the hull's own radius near the tip -- comparing a cap base of 3.7 against the hull's computed radius of roughly 4.18 at that same height, which reveals the cap is actually narrower than the hull surface there, so I need to reconcile how the dome transitions into the cap shape near the tip.

Adding a torus mooring ring too. I'm setting up the lathe geometry with the axis along the hull, checking the outline closes properly back to the axis, and adding a tail cone with navy/gold coloring plus a glowing tail light sphere near the tip. Now I'm extruding the top and bottom fins using local coordinate frames with thickness and bevel for each.

Working out fin outline points to avoid self-intersection, separating the fin shape from the trailing rudder section, and cross-checking where the fin's trailing edge meets the hull radius at that position along the body.

Keeping the leading edge straight for a geometric art-deco feel, with smoothing set to zero. I'm verifying the fin tip stays buried inside the hull radius at x=34, then checking the rudder outline near the tail to see if its root pokes outside the hull boundary at x=1.2.

Since there's a 1.6-unit gap, I'll lower the rudder root's starting y-value so it tucks under the hull curve there, and confirm the four perpendicular rudder fins stay hidden within the hull near the axis before the tail cap extends past them.

Now I'm matching the rudder's trailing edge to where the fin begins at x=8.5, trimming the rudder's run to end slightly earlier for a clean hinge line. For the tail fin I'm setting a thickness taper from root to tip with a beveled edge, then working out the paint scheme—navy base with gold pinstripes, a sunray emblem, and gilded edges along the wall surfaces.

Now I'm giving the rudder an oxblood base with cream horizontal stripes and gold trim, then placing chrome rods along the fin's leading and tip edges by converting the blueprint coordinates into model space. I'm adding colored glow spheres at the fin tips for navigation lights and starting to place emblem decals on the vertical fin surfaces.

I'll put registration text on one fin and keep the emblem on the other, since decals read correctly from either viewing side so mirroring isn't an issue. For the engine nacelles, I'm calculating hull taper positions at two z-stations to find mounting points, then working out the clock-angle placement on the hull surface for where each nacelle attaches.

Working out nacelle offset math...

Still defining nacelle outline...

I'm adding a thin chrome cowl ring lathe shape and a forward-facing art deco grille decal on the nacelle, then considering a small porthole decal on the outer side.

Now I'm shaping the gilded rear spinner cone and building the four-blade propeller geometry, extruding each blade radially outward from the hub with tapered width and smoothing.

For pitch, I'm tilting the tangential width direction slightly so the blades angle properly, giving them thickness and dark wood coloring with gilt tips near the ends, with roots buried inside the spinner. Now I'm planning the support struts connecting the hull to the nacelle tops.

Working out gondola placement at z=24, spanning 11 to 37, I'm calculating the hull's bottom curve at those points to find the clearance gap between the gondola top and hull bottom, which ranges roughly 0.9 to 2.9 units—enough space to add a keel fairing connecting them.

Now I'm sizing that fairing: a loft from z=12 to 35, about 4.5 wide and roughly 4.5 tall, centered so its top buries into the hull and its bottom sits inside the gondola, creating a tapered "keel neck" look with navy coloring and gold ribs for the art deco style, shrinking at both ends so it blends smoothly into the hull and gondola using the loft API.

For the cross-section shape, I'm weighing a smooth elliptical sweep versus a faceted octagonal ngon — ellipses give that rounded Zephyr-style streamline look while ngons would feel more faceted, so I'm leaning toward an ngon-8 section oriented with a vertex pointing up for the forward tube.

I'm sketching out the gondola station widths and heights along the z-axis, tapering from a small rear tip to a wider midsection and narrowing again toward the front, while accounting for how the rounded end cap extends the overall length.

For the cap style, a round sweep end gives a smooth streamlined dome for the nose. I'm checking that the gondola top aligns well inside the fairing bottom, then planning the paint scheme: navy below the belt line, a gold pinstripe at the boundary, and cream above with subtle roof shading, plus some chrome speed-line details.

For those speed lines, I'm thinking they should wrap around the full gondola including the nose and tail, converging toward the front in classic art deco style since the loops intersect both end caps. I'm also placing window decals along the sides of the gondola.

For the window decal itself, I want a repeating texture of rounded windows with gold frames and warm amber glass showing subtle curtain silhouettes, with transparency cutting away the background so the body paint shows through between windows. I'm considering splitting this into two layered decals — a non-glowing gold frame layer and a separately glowing glass layer — so the glow effect only hits the window panes rather than the whole fixture.

For the bridge, I'm planning a wraparound front decal projected onto the nose, drawn as trapezoidal panes with chrome mullions, using a darker navy reflective glass look with highlight streaks rather than full glow, to distinguish it from the warmer glowing passenger windows while still giving it a faint cyan tint.

For the door, I'm placing an art deco sunburst-fan door decal in the rear section, adjusting the window band so it doesn't overlap, positioning the door around z -8.5 with its own size and position separate from the main window strip.

Now I'm adding a chrome searchlight with a glowing lens under the gondola nose, and figuring out how to orient a torus-based bumper wheel so its axle runs along the X axis to roll properly along Z, working out the vertical offset so the tire bottom sits correctly.

For the wheel assembly, I'm planning a hub cylinder, a fork of two rods connecting the wheel axle to the gondola bottom, and a streamlined art-deco wheel fairing (spat) made from an extruded teardrop profile to partially conceal the wheel.

Working out the spat outline so it covers the upper half of the wheel in navy with a gold stripe, leaving the tyre visible below, and aligning its top edge to bury seamlessly into the gondola bottom.

I'll add small chrome hub cap discs on the spat sides at the axle for decoration, since the wheel itself stays hidden inside. Checking the lowest point of the structure—tyre at ground level, gondola bottom at 1.7, engine nacelles higher up—everything lines up correctly, and now I'm positioning the Hindenburg-style passenger window decal strip along the lower hull flank.

I'll set the decal's direction to the surface normal with a slanted size for the promenade windows row, keeping it separate from the navy cheatline band positioned lower on the hull. Then I'll add a name banner higher on the flank near the bow, with "AURORA" lettered in gold with a navy outline and small deco flourishes alongside it.

Working out emblem and banner placement now—positioning the nose roundel so it doesn't overlap the name banner, adding a registration decal on the tail fin, and figuring out how to orient dorsal vents along the hull's top line using tangent-facing path points.

Now I'm adding dorsal surface details: small vent hoods stuck at several points along the top of the hull facing outward, plus a couple of observation blisters near the front, before moving on to gold trim loops around the hull.

I'm placing thin gilt metal bands as decorative loops around the hull near the nose (triple bands) and near the tail, using the surface's natural polygon cross-sections even where fins intersect — confirming that works fine since the loop is just a plane-cut of the hull's triangles.

I'm setting an appropriate drift size for brass/gilt materials (~2.5m scale) so the texture noise doesn't look like speckle at this hull size, keeping the flat color palette under budget. I'm also designing an art deco winged-sunburst emblem decal for the top fin, and thinking about extra gondola details like rear observation windows and a possible antenna wire to the hull.

For the gondola, I'm skipping a radio mast and under-hull antenna, deciding against a flag but adding chrome speed-whisker loops on the sides, a navy keel strip along the bottom, and a gold chevron ornament on the nose using a separate CHEVRON decal texture. I'm also adding small running-board steps under the door and a glowing searchlight lens, while skipping handrail ladders.

Now I'm tallying up the part counts: each nacelle needs a lathed body, cowl, and spinner, four blades, grille and porthole decals, three struts, an exhaust rod, and a small tail fin — thirteen parts times four nacelles is fifty-two. The four fins each get a rudder, leading and tip rods, a light, two decals, and hinge rods, totaling twenty-eight parts. For the hull itself I'm counting the main hull, sixteen battens, a cap, mooring spike and ring, five gold bands, tail cone and light, eight vents, two blisters, and various name/emblem/window decals.

Moving to the gondola, I'm listing its body, fairing, speed loops, window frames and glass, bridge, doors and steps, chevron, searchlights, spat, tyre, and hub caps, and now I'm working out how to place six vertical gold art-deco fluting ribs along the curved fairing surface — figuring out the x and y positions where thin rod boxes should sit against the elliptical cross-section at different heights.

That gives roughly 35 gondola parts, bringing the running total to about 163, which is still short of my 180-340 target range, so I need to think of additional details like a painted hull cheatline or nacelle elements to add more part count.

Adding fairing bumps at fin roots and bumping propeller blades to 16; polygon count stays manageable around 2k triangles. Now I'm working out the decal API for hull banners and lettering — target surface, projection direction, grid segments for the curved hull — and double-checking the sweep function signature for path and radius parameters.

Checking remaining builder APIs...

Writing SVG texture markup...

Now I'm sketching the whiskers on the hull design, then moving to the emblem: a navy roundel with gold ring, sunburst rays, and a stylized "A" center, plus stepped wing feathers extending outward on a wider canvas.

Next I'm designing the gondola window band as separate frame and glass textures -- repeating window units with gold-outlined frames and amber-gradient glass panes featuring curtain silhouettes and lamp dots.

I also realize the hull window strip can reuse these same textures at a different scale rather than making new ones, which saves on texture count. Then I'm planning a bridge texture with a wrapped band of trapezoidal panes, dark blue glass with diagonal highlights, chrome mullions, and a subtle glow.

Deciding against glowing the bridge glass since dark navy would just stay dark anyway. Now sketching out several more decal textures: a navy door with gold frame, sunburst fan window, and chrome handle; a circular chrome grille with horizontal bars for nacelle fronts; and a set of three nested gold chevrons.

Also planning a glowing amber porthole with a brass ring, and registration text "LZ 140" for the bottom fin — bringing the total to ten textures. Now defining the hull color palette...

Still writing paint shader...

Still writing shader logic...

Now I'm checking the cheatline position as it transitions along the hull: the boundary rises toward the nose where it merges into the navy section, and at the banner and emblem locations the cheatline curve stays consistent with the smoothstep blending I set up.

I'm repositioning the emblem to z=46, a=125 to avoid overlapping the gold band, with a winged aspect ratio around 9×4.8. The fins get navy paint with gold pinstripes, the rudder gets red paint with cream horizontal art-deco stripes near the tip, and I'm starting to work out the gondola paint scheme next.

Writing paint functions...

I realize 1.8° of width is only about 6 cm at this radius, too thin to render clearly, so I widen the lines to roughly 3.5° half-width each, tapering them near the rear using a smoothstep on the height range. I'm also confirming the lathe's local axis orientation (+Z forward, +X right) so the side markings stay symmetric at 90°/270°, then moving on to defining the blade outline shape.

Now I'm working out model-space math for the nacelles, defining a helper to normalize z-position along the hull and a sweep function that returns position and normal vectors at a given angle. I'm sketching a nacelle builder that places engine cars on the lower flanks by computing hull points at specific angular offsets and flattening their normals onto the horizontal plane.

I'm checking the angle mapping to confirm symmetry between left and right sides (238° vs 122°, both 32° off the belly line), then working through the arithmetic for the actual x/y coordinates of one nacelle pair using the hull radius, offset distance, and normal direction.

For pair B at z=-30, the hull radius shrinks, giving a different nacelle position that's nicely staggered from pair A. I'm also checking whether the pusher propeller on the rear of pair A, with its disk radius, clears the hull surface at that point along the fuselage.

Now I'm working out the strut geometry connecting hull to nacelle, computing endpoint offsets along the normal direction and vertical span at each strut.

Still defining strut placement...

For the propeller, I'm setting up four blades in an X arrangement, computing radial and tangential directions per blade angle and tilting them slightly, with the hub positioned behind the nacelle center.

Checking the spinner geometry against the nacelle radius to make sure the hub blends smoothly into the cone tip, then I'm moving on to work out the gondola position along the Z axis.

Now I'm mapping out the fairing cross-sections at each Z station, tracking how the width and height taper from the nose toward the main body so it blends under the hull without colliding with the gondola's front profile.

Checking the vertical clearance, I find the fairing's rear bottom edge actually dips below the gondola's top surface near the rear cap, creating a small overlap gap. I'll correct this by lowering the fairing station at that point so it clears the gondola properly.

Checking both rear and front positions confirms the fairing top stays buried beneath the hull in both cases, so the geometry works. For the gondola loft, I'm uncertain whether sweep options like sides and smooth apply the same way, but I'll pass them through anyway and see if the loft function accepts them.

Widths run along X and heights along Y, so I need to keep that orientation consistent. For the loft caps I'll specify round caps explicitly. For the window decal on the gondola, I'm checking that the window band (y 4.6-6.3) fits within the flat side face of the octagonal cross-section, which spans roughly y 3.46-5.94 -- so the windows slightly overshoot that flat region and I need to adjust.

I'll narrow the window band to center at y=5.0 with height 1.5 (so 4.25-5.75) to stay inside the flat face. I'm placing the belt navy below 3.25, gold from 3.25-3.5, chrome speed loops at y=3.7 and 3.95, and a gold loop above the windows at y=6.25, then positioning the door centered at y=4.1 with size 1.7x3.0.

Now I'm figuring out the gondola's front nose section—checking the width at various z positions to size a bridge decal and dome windows near the rounded cap, working out whether the projection direction for the windows grid should run along -Z from the nose tip.

Then narrowing further to z13 w4.4 h4.4 at the cap for the nose tip near ZG+15.2, with the bridge band positioned around y5.2-6.3. The decal projected onto the taper region naturally wraps since rays hit the sides at the earlier station, giving a wraparound effect without extra work. I'll add a chevron decal near the nose's lower dome area, and now I'm thinking through placing a small searchlight cylinder underneath the nose.

For the searchlight itself, I'm placing a short chrome cylinder tucked just under the gondola's front bottom so it's buried slightly into the hull, with a glowing lens disc on its forward face for the light effect. The geometry checks out — the cylinder's top sits above the gondola's bottom edge, so it reads as mounted rather than floating.

Now I'm sketching rear stabilizer fins: small chrome blades jutting sideways near the gondola's rear, positioned along narrowing fuselage stations, outlined as thin tapered shapes sticking out from the hull surface to suggest little speed fins.

Settling on a gold stylized tail shape, three per side at varying heights. Now I'm figuring out fairing ribs—placing small box struts around the fairing surface at regular intervals along the z-axis, using surface-hit queries to position them flush against the hull.

Adding hull vents next, placing steel boxes along the top ridge of the hull at various parametric positions, checking that they embed properly into the sloped facets.

Still working out the vent cap placement...

I'm considering whether to add dorsal observation blisters near the hull top but deciding to skip for now and focus on hull passenger window decals instead, positioning them at symmetric angles around the hull.

Nacelles at z -6 and -30, x 18.5, y 14 fall within hull windows at z 13..31, so that's clear. For the name banner, I'm placing it with a=118 giving deg left 298, right 62, centered around t 0.656 with size [30, 5], while the emblem sits at z 44 (t .844), a=122, deg left 302, right 58, size [8.5, 4.5] — banner spans z 5..35 and emblem 39.75..48.25, so they fit without overlap. Text orientation should follow world Y on each side, and I'm thinking the registration "LZ 140" could go on the bottom fin on both sides instead of the aft flank.

I'm figuring out decal placement on the bottom fin by converting local fin coordinates into model space, checking that the decal sits outside the fin's thin face so it doesn't clip, and sizing it to [9, 2.6]. For the top fin emblem, I'm doing the same coordinate conversion at x=19, y=14, sized [11, 5.9], but I need to make sure the decal footprint stays within the fin's actual outline since oversized decals might fail to project correctly onto the surface.

That fits within the rudder bound at x=8.5. Now I'm placing the registration marking on the bottom fin, centered at (19, 14.5) with size [8, 2.2], since the emblem occupies the top fin only.

I also need to add emblem decals on the top face of both horizontal fins, oriented with direction [0,1,0] and up vector [0,0,1] so they're visible from above and point forward. I'm working out the model-space coordinates for the left fin's emblem placement, then mapping the fin's outline extrusion using its origin point and direction vectors before moving on to the fin's paint scheme with navy and gold pinstripes.

Writing paint shader logic...

Now I want to add a cream stripe tracing the leading edge, so I'm working out the signed distance from a point to the leading-edge line using the line's direction vector and normal, then checking the sign convention with a sample interior point to confirm which side is "inside" the fin.

I'm defining a lighting helper that blends a base color toward a warm tone when the normal faces up and toward a cool tone when it faces down, giving the surface subtle directional shading.

Now I'm setting up metal paint variants for gilt, chrome, and brass with specific noise sizing and polish values, then working out the tail cone geometry—lathing a navy cap profile at the rear of the hull where the radius tapers down to meet the base.

I'm checking whether the rudders overlap the tail cone's radius envelope (they do partially, but that's acceptable since the rudders start outside the cone), placing a white glowing light sphere near the cone tip, and adding chrome hinge rods along the rudder root line. I'm skipping the fin root fairings and moving on to mooring details next.

Now I'm adding the nose spike and a mooring collar: a tapered spike extends forward from the nose cap, and I'm wrapping a torus ring around its base to act as an attachment collar rather than a hanging eye.

For the battens, I'm placing 16 raised ribs at 22.5° intervals along the hull near the nose, aligning them with the gold ray paint so they read as gilded ribs on the surface — these taper off right under the nose cap. Now I'm setting positions for the gold accent bands further back along the hull.

For the bands and loops, I'm placing closed gold sweep loops at several z-positions along the hull, including near the tail fins, each defined by a loop curve on the hull's surface with radius 0.3 and gilt coloring — and confirming no caps are needed since the paths are closed. I'm also noting that static models can skip joints entirely, which simplifies things, and checking that decals and surfaces still work fine without them before moving on to the gondola speed loops.

Now I'm working through the gondola details: adding a thin chrome loop around the body, deciding to skip a keel strip since the navy paint covers that area anyway, confirming the mid-roof meets the fairing properly, and placing a rear lounge window decal near the back of the gondola.

I'm also sizing the rear end cap of the gondola, then adding small glowing red and green navigation lights near the front sides, and sketching in a step box beneath the entry door along the lower belly.

Now I'm turning to engine car details — a porthole decal on the outer nacelle side, a front grille decal sized to cover the lathe-shaped dome tip, making sure the circular pattern stays transparent outside its radius so it fits the nacelle's tapered front profile.
